messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajiv is a 76-year-old South Asian man who has worked as an electrician for most of his adult life, a trade that has kept him physically active and socially embedded in his community well into his seventies. He lives with his wife in a quiet residential neighbourhood and, until recently, had maintained a steady routine of early morning starts and weekend visits to the local market. That routine collapsed approximately eight months ago, when Rajiv was robbed at knifepoint on a Friday evening while walking home from a hardware store. Two men approached him quickly from behind in a narrow side street; one grabbed his arm and shoved him against a wall while the other pressed close, filling the air with the sharp smell of alcohol. They took his wallet and phone, and when Rajiv tried to speak, the man holding the knife moved it closer to his face. The entire encounter lasted perhaps ninety seconds. He walked the rest of the way home shaking, and told his wife he was fine.

He was not fine. In the weeks that followed, Rajiv began waking in the early hours from nightmares in which the details of the robbery replayed in distorted but recognisable form — the sudden grip on his arm, the smell, the wall at his back. What he noticed, and what began to trouble him most, was what happened in those first moments after waking. The residue of the dream did not dissolve when he opened his eyes. Instead, the sense of danger felt immediate and unresolved, as though the men were still close. He had come to believe, in those night-time moments, that the darkness of his own bedroom was genuinely unsafe — that something threatening remained present just beyond his perception. This bleed from sleep into waking meant that nights became their own ordeal, and his sense that the world was less safe after dark deepened steadily over the following months. He now finds it genuinely harder to feel safe at night than during the day, a distinction that feels not irrational to him but simply accurate, a lesson the robbery confirmed.

The same logic extended outward into his waking life. The robbery had happened because two men had approached him from behind in an ordinary setting — not a dangerous neighbourhood, not late at night, simply a street he had walked dozens of times. That fact lodged in him as a permanent revision of how the world worked. Now, when strangers approach him in ordinary situations — at the hardware supplier where he still occasionally picks up materials for small jobs, in the car park outside the supermarket, even in the corridor of his own building — he feels a spike of threat that he cannot talk himself out of. A neighbour reaching past him on a shelf, a delivery driver walking quickly toward him: his body responds before his mind can intervene. Sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard, a reaction that has made the practical side of his work increasingly difficult. Electricians work in close quarters with other tradespeople, and Rajiv has found himself flinching or stepping sharply back when a colleague moves unexpectedly, which has drawn comment and, once, a direct question from a younger man on a job site. He deflected it, but the incident shamed him.

Crowded places have become nearly impossible. The market he once visited every weekend now strikes him as a space full of unpredictable movement and unknown people pressing close — conditions that his nervous system now reads as threat. He has stopped going. His wife does the shopping alone.

The smell of alcohol, encountered on a stranger's breath or near a pub doorway, produces an immediate and visceral return of the robbery's atmosphere — and with it, the same heightened sense of danger that the nightmares leave behind. This olfactory trigger, like waking from a dream, does not merely remind him of what happened; it convinces him, briefly and bodily, that something like it is about to happen again.

Rajiv sought help not after any single episode but after his wife told him quietly that she was worried. He is hoping, cautiously, to feel safe in ordinary places again. What he fears most is that he will not.
